newsitem.title: UK: Outlook for UK sugar beet crop improved after rain.
newsitem.headline: Outlook for UK sugar beet crop improved after rain.

text.p: Recent rains over Britain's sugar beet growing areas have helped reverse the effects of earlier dry weather and the initial gloomy prognosis for this year's crop, beet experts said on Friday.

The latest British beet test, as conducted by British Sugar plc, showed amounts of sugar per root and root weights were both above the equivalent test in 1995, although percentage contents were still lower.
At the start of the test cycle in early August, analysts said the crop needed moisture in areas with lighter soils, although the beet was not suffering from stress.
"It (the crop) is making nice progress...it's promising. The rains in the recent weeks...have been just what the crop needs," said an official at the National Farmers Union (NFU).
"It's got along much better than I anticipated last week to this week. It's all down to the weather," she said.
British Sugar has said the crop has made good progress and is on course for an average result but has declined to give any output estimate or the number of beets sown per hectare.
The first beet processing factories are set to open on September 30 after the conclusion of the field test cycle.

"So far everything has been going reasonably well -- the rain has helped the crop considerably and the harvest is due to start in early October," said Simon Kerr of the National Institute of Agricultural Botany.

Although this year's crop is believed to be generally healthy so far, with an absence of the principal virus yellows disease, analysts have said it could still be threatened by moths from a plague earlier in the summer.

Incidence of such diseases as red spider and powdery mildew is said to have been low, although earlier in its growing cycle the crop suffered an invasion of silver Y moths, which produce beet-grazing green caterpillars.
